newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU opens full probe into Boeing-McDonnell merger.
newsitem.headline: EU opens full probe into Boeing-McDonnell merger.

text.p: The European Commission said on Wednesday it was starting a full probe into the proposed merger of Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp to create the world's largest aerospace group.

The move was widely expected, including by Boeing, because the merger of the two U.S. companies is too big to be nodded through by the European Union's competition watchdog after only an initial one-month review.

Analysts and anti-trust experts think it will be approved finally without any substantial changes because McDonnell Douglas is no longer a serious aerospace contender and the alliance is believed to have the backing of the Pentagon, the U.S. defence department.

"This deal is a U.S. deal and Europe is not particularly well placed to enforce any conditions," John Boyce, a partner with law firm Slaughter & May, told Reuters. "But it needs to have the full probe to ensure Europe is not forgotten."

The alliance, which consists in Boeing taking over its ailing defence and space rival through a share-swap operation valued in December at $13.3 billion, is also being investigated by the U.S. Federal Trade Commission.
One competition expert also thought any remedies were likely to be agreed between the antitrust authorities on the two sides of the Atlantic.
"The idea of some sort of honourable settlement is one which is going through people's mind," he said, asking not to be named.
The EU and the U.S. Department of Justice have closely cooperated in the past on compeition issues and are said to be on good terms.

"The Commission will, in particular, have to examine to what extent Boeing's leading position in the market for commercial jet aircraft could be strengthened by the proposed merger," the Commission said in a statement.
Boeing has 60 percent of the world's market for commercial airliners of more than 100 seats, the Commission said.

It noted the deal would represent a further increase in Boeing's market share leaving only one competitor -- the European Airbus consortium of Germany's Daimler-Benz Aerospace , Aerospatiale of France, British Aerospace and Spain's Construcciones Aeronauticas.
The Commission was also concerned the alliance with McDonnell would give Boeing greater access to the space and defence business, strengthening its power over aircraft equipment suppliers.

"The Commission will...need to investigate to what extent the large increase in Boeing's defence and space business could strengthen its market position in commercial aircraft, for example in terms of overall financial resources, greater access to technology developed in the defence and space sector, and increased bargaining power vis-a-vis equipment suppliers," the statement said.

The comment was seen as a clear reference to recent allegations that Boeing had leaned on a potential U.S. Airbus suppliers interested in joining the consortium's planned A3XX super jumbo project. The project is intended to rival the long-standing dominance of Boeing's 747 passenger jet .
But whatever the Commission's final conclusions, lawyers and other competition watchers were sceptical about what the Commission could do.

The Commission has in the past forced companies to reduce the scope of their merger plans to avoid creation or strengthening of dominant positions in the EU. But the Boeing, McDonnell case is different because the companies do not have any assets in Europe, except for maintaining and repairing aircraft.

Boeing chairman and chief executive officer Phil Condit said last week in Brussels, where he met European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert, that he was expecting the alliance to clear all regulatory hurdles by July.

The Commission, which has a maximum of four months to reach a decision, has the power to investigate corporate mergers and takeovers involving companies with a combined worldwide turnover of five billion European currency units and European sales of at least 250 million Ecus each. This also applies to deals involving only non-EU companies.
